claims.text: Increasing configurational entropy during synthesis stabilizes a single-phase structure in noble metal–based HEA nanomaterials.
Increasing configurational entropy promotes uniform atomic mixing in noble metal–based HEA nanomaterials.
A single-phase, uniformly mixed structure is critical for reliable material formation.
A single-phase, uniformly mixed structure enhances catalytic performance relative to lower-entropy binary or ternary counterparts.
The initial material is a mixed-metal precursor containing noble metals but not yet converted into a homogeneous alloy phase.
Annealing at approximately 600°C for 1 hour in an inert or reducing atmosphere activates atomic diffusion.
Annealing under these conditions promotes high-entropy mixing.
The controlled comparison uses identical temperature, atmosphere, and annealing time for HEA and lower-entropy compositions.
High configurational entropy favors atomic intermixing during annealing.
Entropy-driven atomic intermixing suppresses phase separation.
Suppression of phase separation produces a homogeneous surface distribution of active noble-metal sites.
A homogeneous distribution of active noble-metal sites lowers reaction activation barriers.
Lower reaction activation barriers enhance catalytic activity.
Relative to binary alloys, HEA nanomaterials will show a more uniformly mixed, single-phase morphology.
Relative to binary alloys, HEA nanomaterials will show lower onset potentials and higher current densities.
Binary or ternary alloy nanomaterials typically exhibit more phase segregation than HEA nanomaterials processed under the same conditions.
Binary or ternary alloy nanomaterials typically have a less uniform distribution of catalytic sites than HEA nanomaterials.
The hypothesis is expected to apply under high-temperature annealing in inert or reducing atmospheres and in systems without major impurities.
Changes in annealing temperature or atmosphere may produce different phase behavior.
